artifacts.summary: Recommends extending guard-destructive-git.sh's over-staging predicate with a per-token check (trailing-slash primary; filesystem -d and glob-metachar as low-cost general-rule extensions) inside the existing ADD_SEGMENTS loop, confirms git-commit-scoped.sh's internal directory-pathspec git add is invisible to the hook (no conflict, no exemption needed), and documents the quoted-pathspec blind spot inherent in reusing COMMAND_SCAN as an accepted pre-existing-shaped limitation.

memory_candidates.content: guard-destructive-git.sh's PreToolUse hook only ever observes the literal top-level tool_input.command string of a Bash call. Any git add/commit invoked as a subprocess inside a wrapper script (e.g. git-commit-scoped.sh's internal `git add "${task_dir}/"` with a directory pathspec) is structurally invisible to the hook and needs no exemption -- this is the established, reusable pattern (already documented for git-snapshot.sh's internal `git add -A`) for any future sanctioned command that would otherwise trip a Bash-level guard.

guard-destructive-git.sh's upfront COMMAND_SCAN quote-strip (sed 's/"[^"]*"/""/g') replaces an ENTIRE quoted span with literal empty quotes before any detector runs. This correctly neutralizes commit-message false positives (e.g. -m "fix -a bug"), but as a side effect erases any legitimate quoted git-add pathspec argument too, so a quoted directory/glob pathspec (git add -- "some/dir/") bypasses detection -- the same pre-existing blind spot already affects the bare-dot check (git add "." is not caught either). Any future detector reusing COMMAND_SCAN inherits this same quoted-argument blind spot; it is a structural tradeoff of the shared quote-strip, not a per-detector bug.
